what_it_does: AI accelerator chips — specialized processors designed just for running neural networks — are expensive, and it would be wasteful to dedicate an entire chip to a single small job. This paper looks at chips that are built as a grid of cores (processing units) connected by an internal communication network, like the Graphcore IPU or Tenstorrent chips, and asks: can we safely share one of these chips among several AI jobs at once? The complication is that the cores need to pass data to each other over fixed internal routes, so splitting the chip naively breaks those communication paths. vNPU introduces three coordinated techniques: it creates virtual (software-defined) routing paths that redirect each job's data flow to the physical cores actually assigned to it; it translates memory addresses in a way that respects the chip's internal network layout to avoid stalls; and it searches over possible assignments of virtual cores to physical cores to find one that balances workloads well. The result, validated on a hardware emulator, is that multiple jobs can share the chip with better combined throughput than naive partitioning.
